newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Can Freelander jump-start Rover to profitability?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Can Freelander jump-start Rover to profitability?.

text.p: When Rover Group first met BMW it may have been love at first sight for the British, but the German car giant had only one thing on its mind -- Land Rover's attractive profit margins.

The courtship was even captured on film for a British television documentary. Now three years into their union, Rover is about to deliver its first new product from the relationship -- the baby Land Rover.

The Freelander is the result of the injection of billions of pounds of BMW investment and its world-renowned technical know-how into Rover. The launch next year will be key to BMW's objective to make Rover Group profitable by the year 2000.
"Freelander will be a major factor in whether we hit that target," said Bernard Carey, Rover board member and director of external affairs.
"Every new product is vital to achieving that ambition. But it is particularly so with Freelander because it's not replacing a model. It is a new product and market for us to be in," he told Reuters.
Arthur Maher, head of research at LMC International, sister motor analyst to the influential J D Power, agrees Freelander could make or break Rover's turnaround.

"Freelander is going to be fundamental...Land Rover is the jewel in the crown of the Group. The 4x4 division has done very well with Discovery but Land Rover is looking for the next improvement in sales and product," he said.
"This is particularly important to BMW as it looks to take on Mercedes new 'M' class (of 4x4 vehicles) which is new, more upmarket, prestigious and close in pricing to LR products," Maher added.
FILLS GAP IN LAND ROVER PORTFOLIO
Freelander will fill a crucial gap in Land Rover's vehicle portfolio. In recent years offroaders have seen pacy growth in Europe, but more so in the United States.
One of the fastest growing sub-divisions in the sector has been the smaller offroader or sports utility vehicle.

As other manufacturers were scooping up sales, LR was losing out. Bill Baker, Land Rover's newly appointed director of corporate affairs and one of the key figures involved in the strategic launch of Freelander, summed up:
"The reason we developed Freelander was because there was this key sector of less expensive, lighter vehicles and we weren't in it."

"Freelander had started out using technology from the car side of the business. But as it developed it had more Land Rover capabilities built into its brief and now has some off road capability." Baker told Reuters.
Baker, a former vice-president of Land Rover North America, said it would be priced at between 15,000 pounds ($24,500) and 21,000 pounds, with a three and five door available.
WORLD ROLL-OUT BEGINS JANUARY 1998
The Freelander will be launched in Britain in January 1998 and then roll out to Europe, eventually being sold in South Africa, Australia, southeast Asia and eventually Japan.

Who will Freelander appeal to? "We see it attracting a younger buyer, one who is successful but not yet at the peak of their earning capability. The three door will appeal to the single market and the five door to couples."
Baker said Land Rover saw Freelander making up the biggest chunk of its sales in future.

Carey outlined the world launch timetable for the baby Land Rover. "We expect to launch in the UK in January and roll-out across Europe in the spring. Outside of Europe, in the first year we are looking to launch in our other markets. Except for Japan which comes in 1999."
Carey said the delayed launch there was because Japan is an automatic vehicle market and this type of gearbox will not be available immediately.

Rover sources expect first year European sales to be between 35,000 and 50,000 Freelanders. Outside Europe the target is 10,000 to 20,000, with four to five thousand expected to be sold in its Japanese debut year.
LAND ROVER CASHCOW OF GROUP
The margins on Land Rover products are hefty and remain the lifeblood of the rest of Rover itself.

"The volumes for this business may not be huge, but the business has been consistently solid and profitable for the group and its dealers," said Baker. "It's the cashcow of the group and has been the success story even while other parts of Rover were imploding."
Maher believes Europe can never see the kind of volume growth seen in the U.S. market where offroaders and similar classed vehicles have 40 percent of total sales.
"In Europe, the segment has gone nowhere near the U.S. growth levels because fuel is expensive and these are thirsty vehicles and European countries tax large engine vehicles heavily," said Maher.

LMC said total European sports utility sales grew to 327,625 vehicles in 1996 from 174,221 in 1991. By 2000 European sales are seen at 479,012. LMC predicts that LR's Freelander will sell just 13,904 in 1998, rising to a peak of 32,857 in 1999 and slipping to 26,673 by 2002.
STRONG STERLING COULD STING MARGINS
But as Rover gears up for the launch it faces one possibly major setback to its sales targets -- the surging pound.
Sterling has risen 20 percent against the Deutsche mark since last summer and is already causing widespread pain across Britain's export industry.
Carey concedes "It's not good news. It will be a squeeze and we will have to push hard to reduce costs."

Walter Hasselkus, Rover chairman, said last year "The baby Land Rover is very much an export product." So concern about the pound overpricing Freelander overseas is genuine, with 70 percent of production seen for export.

Maher says Rover has no choice but to take the currency hit. "It will put a spanner in the works. Rover must ask -- do we take it on the chin and cut margins or do we downgrade the specification of the vehicle. That's not an option when you are in launch mode.
"So national sales chiefs across Europe will say to Rover - price competitively at local level. But if Rover does that, it has implications for BMW's profitability."
($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
